title: VerveCloud private onramp / VPC design intake
topics: Throughput and latency SLOs for inference
summary: Intro discovery between Redwood AE/SE and VerveCloud engineering to scope private onramp. Key concerns: cross-account peering, IP planning, egress NAT and controlled outbound, KMS/HSM integration, SOC2/compliance artifacts, and multi-region latency targeting. Next steps agreed: share network checklist, sample VPC route table diagram, and schedule a focused SE deep-dive on KMS and canary rollout plan.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2029-01-14 10:30 AM PT / 18:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: John (Redwood AE), Lina (Redwood SE), Maya (CTO, VerveCloud), Tom (Network Lead), Priya (Head of Security), Ethan (Platform Eng)

Summary (auto): Quick intake to align on private onramp requirements and network constraints. We drilled into peering options, private endpoints, KMS, and regional gating.

[00:00] John (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick round robin, then Lina and I will jump into the network checklist and questions. Maya, you want to kick off with the business context?
[00:10] Maya (CTO): Yeah thanks John. We're evaluating Redwood for model serving — main asks are we need private connectivity from our VPCs into Redwood, strict data residency for EU traffic, and KMS integration so keys never leave our control. We're also trying to limit any public egress.
[00:26] John: Got it. Our private onramp supports VPC peering and private endpoints, also transit gateway setups for scale — Lina will explain tradeoffs.
[00:35] Lina (SE): Hi all. A couple clarifying q's up front: how many AWS accounts / regions will call Redwood? And do you have a preferred path — direct peering, AWS PrivateLink, or Transit Gateway?
[00:46] Tom (Network): We have two prod accounts and a separate networking account with a TGW. Production spans us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Ideally we want a single egress point per region and strict egress NAT so outbound IPs are predictable for allowlists.
[01:05] Priya (Security): Also need to understand audit log retention and separation of customer metadata. SOC2 is table stakes for us.
[01:12] Lina: Totally. On peering: VPC peering is simplest for low-latency single-account connections but doesn't scale well cross-account. PrivateLink gives private endpoints and simpler DNS management but can be more operational with ENIs and cross-AZ scaling. Transit Gateway can centralize egress and peering attachments — works well with your networking account and TGW topology.
[01:36] Ethan (Platform): Curious about IP address consumption. We have pretty tight /16 allocations in prod and don't want to carve massive extra ranges.
[01:43] Lina: We'll provide an IP plan template. Redwood can work with either small endpoint subnets for PrivateLink or larger peered ranges for VPC peering. We also support IP slicing (e.g., NAT gateway per-subnet) to reduce address usage.
[01:58] John: To be concrete, can you share your current CIDRs and route tables — Tom? That will help Lina give a tailored recommendation.
[02:05] Tom: Yeah we'll export and send. One more — do you support cross-account TGW attachments? We want Redwood in a different account.
[02:14] Lina: Yes, we support cross-account TGW peering and attachments. There's a couple of approaches: Redwood can host a managed account that's attached to your TGW, or you can peer to Redwood's VPCs via peering/privatelink. For security-conscious customers we often recommend PrivateLink in combination with TGW to centralize control in the networking account.
[02:36] Priya: For KMS, do you require keys in our account? We cannot hand keys over.
[02:41] Lina: We integrate with customer-managed keys (CMK) in your KMS. You can provision the key in your account and grant Redwood a crypto-only IAM role for envelope decryption, or use an HSM-backed key — we have examples for both. We'll share a short runbook.
[03:00] Maya: What's the model for logs and audit? We need request-level audit for compliance and to investigate model drift incidents.
[03:07] John: Redwood logs token-level events and request traces — we can expose those logs to your CloudWatch or S3 via a private delivery pipeline, or push them to your SIEM via private endpoints. Retention is configurable; we'll share our SOC2 docs and what fields are included.
[03:24] Tom: On DNS — if we use PrivateLink, we want automatic private DNS override so api.redwood.example goes to the ENI IPs. Is that supported?
[03:31] Lina: Yes, we support the private DNS option with PrivateLink and will provide the instructions for the route 53 private hosted zone. Caveat: if you have split-horizon DNS or strict internal DNS controls, there are additional steps we'll outline.
[03:48] Ethan: Latency SLOs — for our user-facing features we need p50 < 60ms and p95 < 250ms for short chat requests. How does Redwood ensure regional routing?
[03:58] Lina: We can pin traffic to region-local endpoints. For hosted mode we route by latency and cost, but for Private deployments we keep traffic regional per your constraints. We also have fallbacks to a lower-cost variant if capacity in a region is exceeded, but we can disable automatic fallback for stricter compliance.
[04:21] Maya: So if eu-west saturates, you won't route eu traffic to us-east unless we permit?
[04:26] Lina: Correct, we respect region gating. We'll show the policy config.
[04:33] John: Another question — are you planning to use Redwood Hosted or Redwood Dedicated / Private?
[04:38] Maya: We're leaning Private (customer-managed control plane or VPC onramp). We want isolation and to meet EU residency rules. Also cost predictability for a high throughput inference path.
[04:48] Priya: On encryption in transit — do you terminate TLS at Redwood or can we provide mTLS certs for mutual auth?
[04:56] Lina: We support mTLS for PrivateLink endpoints and can accept customer-provided certificates for mutual TLS termination at the private endpoint. We'll include a sample cert rotation plan.
[05:10] Tom: What's the recommended approach for egress? We want to prevent any calls from leaving via public NAT — only allowed egress to our internal logging endpoints and to approved third parties.
[05:20] Lina: You can configure NAT egress controls on your side in front of Redwood, and we support route table policies so that all outbound is via approved IPs. If you need to allowlist Redwood's outbound IPs for downstream services, we can give a predictable set of egress IP ranges per region for private deployments.
[05:38] John: Quick aside — have you looked at other vendors?
[05:42] Maya: We did a short POC with BigCloudAI; their latency was ok but their compliance docs weren't solid. We also have an internal prototype that lacks auto-scaling.
[05:53] Lina: Understood. For scaling, Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools and autoscaling policies — we can discuss quotas and canary rollouts for model version changes.
[06:06] Ethan: Canary logic — how do we route a small percentage of traffic to new model versions without going through public endpoints?
[06:12] Lina: We support in-line canaries at the router level. For Private deployments, the canary is configured in the control plane and enforced at the edge that your VPC peers into — traffic stays internal. We'll share the rollout configuration snippet.
[06:30] Maya: One more: network MTU and jumbo frames. We have some high-throughput batch requests and want to avoid fragmentation.
[06:38] Lina: Our infra supports standard MTU sizes; if you require jumbo frames we can validate path MTU end-to-end during pre-onboarding networking test. We'll add that to the checklist.
[06:50] Tom: OK, practical ask: can you produce a sample architecture diagram showing TGW attachment -> private endpoint -> Redwood ingestion VPC with route tables and security groups?
[07:00] John: Yes, we'll include a diagram and a sample terraform snippet for the PrivateLink endpoint and TGW attachment.
[07:10] Priya: Regarding audit and retention — do you provide field-level redaction or token masking for logs? We don't want PII in any request logs that exit our environment.
[07:20] Lina: We support configurable logging filters and can redact user-provided fields. For strict PII avoidance, you can opt to route logs only to your S3 and disable certain internal logs — we'll document options.
[07:34] Ethan: If we do the managed account approach, how does IAM work? We don't want broad cross-account roles.
[07:40] Lina: Managed account is optional. We prefer cross-account roles with very narrow permissions: crypto-only for KMS decrypt, S3 Put for log delivery (if applicable), and assume-role for deployment actions. We'll provide an IAM least-privilege template.
[07:58] Maya: Timeline — we're aiming to decide vendor and start a pilot in Q1. Our compliance review has a gating milestone end of January. Can you turn materials around quickly?
[08:08] John: Yes. Lina and I will prioritize the network checklist, SOC2/KMS docs, and an architecture diagram. Expect to receive them by Friday.
[08:17] Tom: We'll send the CIDR list and TGW attachments tomorrow.
[08:22] Priya: We'll compile a short list of compliance questions; Lina, can you put the SOC2 whitepaper link in the follow-up?
[08:29] Lina: Absolutely. We'll include cert scans and the encryption whitepaper.
[08:34] John: Anything else?
[08:36] Maya: One last thing — cost model: how do we benchmark token cost and throughput for batch inference? We want to estimate monthly spend for 200M tokens.
[08:46] Lina: We have a cost analyzer and can run a short load test in a dedicated pool to give a TCO estimate. For the pilot we usually do a small benchmark run to capture p50/p95 and throughput.
[08:58] John: Great. Recap of next steps: John will send network checklist and IP plan; Lina will send KMS runbook, SOC2 docs, and terraform snippets; VerveCloud will send CIDRs and TGW map; both teams to schedule a deeper SE call next week.
[09:14] Maya: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[09:18] Tom: Thanks.
[09:20] Priya: Bye.

End transcript.
